title: How to wear a rudraksha mala: common traditions to follow
description: First-wear rituals, the best day to start, thread vs chain, when people remove it, and daily habits: common rudraksha traditions explained simply.
intro: Most families start wearing a rudraksha mala on a Monday morning after a bath, with a short prayer to Shiva, and then keep a few simple habits around it. Beyond that, the rules change a lot from one home to the next. Below are the customs you will hear about most often, so you can pick the ones that fit your family's practice, plus a few practical points for chain-style malas.

sections.heading: Before the first wear: a simple start
paragraphs: There is no single required ritual, but this sequence is common across many North and South Indian homes. Treat it as a guide, not a checklist you must complete.
list: Choose the day. Monday is linked with Shiva, so it is the usual pick. Mahashivratri, a Pradosh day or the start of Shravan are also popular.
Bathe first and wear clean clothes.
Place the mala in front of a picture or idol of Shiva, or near your home mandir.
Some families sprinkle a little Gangajal on it. Others offer flowers or light a diya beside it.
Chant Om Namah Shivaya, commonly 9, 11 or 108 times, then put the mala on.
If your family has a priest, many people simply ask him to do a short puja and hand the mala over.

sections.heading: Thread, chain or metal caps?
paragraphs: Traditional japa malas are strung on red or yellow cotton, or on silk. Thread is light and quiet, but it does wear out and needs restringing every so often. Wool thread is used in some regions too.

Chain malas, where beads are set along a metal chain, are easier for daily wear and less likely to snap. Some people prefer gold or silver caps on each bead, which also protect the bead ends. There is no religious ranking between these; it mostly comes down to how you will use the mala. If you plan to chant on it, choose thread. If you plan to wear it all day with office or casual clothes, a chain is more practical.

sections.heading: How it should sit
paragraphs: Many people believe rudraksha should touch the skin, so they wear it inside the kurta or shirt rather than over it. Others are happy to wear it on top, especially chain styles with a pendant meant to be seen. Both are common.

As a rough guide, a mala that reaches the middle of the chest is comfortable for most people. Very short lengths can feel tight when you bend, and very long ones swing and catch on things. If you wear a wrist mala, check that it slides over your hand easily without being so loose that it slips off.

sections.heading: When some people take it off
paragraphs: This is where practices differ the most. Some traditions say a mala, once worn, need not be removed at all. Others follow a few occasions when they take it off and keep it in a clean place:
list: Before sleeping, placing it near the mandir or under the pillow in a cloth pouch.
While attending a cremation or during a period of mourning.
Before eating non-vegetarian food or drinking alcohol, in families that follow this.
Before using the toilet, in some stricter households.
During swimming, heavy workouts or any activity where it might break.

sections.heading: Small habits that show respect
paragraphs: A rudraksha mala is traditionally treated as personal. Many people do not lend it or let others wear it, though gifting a new one is very common. When you take it off, place it somewhere clean rather than on the floor or a bathroom shelf. If you use it for japa, many traditions say you should not cross the guru bead; instead you turn the mala around and continue in the other direction.

If a bead cracks or the thread breaks, there is no reason to panic. Collect the beads, restring them or keep the cracked bead aside respectfully. Some families immerse old beads in flowing water or place them in a temple; others keep them at the mandir.

sections.heading: A note on chain malas with plated pendants
paragraphs: If your mala has a gold-plated pendant, like the [Om, Trishul and Ganesha chain malas at Varaha](/divine), a couple of the rituals above need small changes. Sprinkle Gangajal rather than soaking the mala, and wipe it dry afterwards. Avoid bathing with it on, and keep perfume and sanitiser away from the chain. These steps help the plating last, and they do not take anything away from the devotion behind wearing it.

faq.q: Which day is best to wear rudraksha for the first time?
faq.a: Monday is the most common choice because it is linked with Shiva. Mahashivratri and days in Shravan month are also popular.

faq.q: Can I sleep wearing a rudraksha mala?
faq.a: Traditions differ. Some never remove it, others take it off at night and keep it near the mandir. Follow your family's practice.

faq.q: Can I wear rudraksha during periods?
faq.a: Views vary widely by family and region. Many people today see no issue, while some households follow restrictions. Ask an elder you trust.
